links.targetTitle: The Governance Point must confirm every Executive Vote item

title: Voting against an Executive Vote containing only already-approved content is an integrity breach
content:
Item 6 in the Tier 2 list at A.1.6.6.1.2 is easy to skim past and is the most conceptually aggressive entry: "Voting against an Executive Vote that only contains content already approved in the Atlas and does not fail Spell validation." It sits among unsubstantiated accusations, proven dishonesty, collusion to manipulate outcomes, kickbacks, and opsec violations — and like all Tier 2 breaches, it means immediate derecognition.

The claim embedded here is that Executive Votes of this specific kind are **not** decision points. If a Spell implements only what the Atlas already approved, and it passes validation, then the only questions a delegate could legitimately be answering are already settled: was this approved (yes) and is the implementation valid (yes). A no vote in that situation cannot be a policy disagreement, because there is no policy at issue — it is an attempt to block execution of a decision already made.

That is why it is classified as integrity rather than procedure. It is treated as an act of obstruction, and obstruction of the execution layer by a delegate holding others' voting power is functionally an attack on the governance dynamic — the category A.1.5.3 names as misalignment.

The two conditions are the safeguard, and they are conjunctive. If the Spell contains anything *not* already approved, the vote is a real decision and opposing it is fully legitimate. If the Spell fails validation, voting against it is arguably obligatory. So the rule bites only in the narrow case where the delegate has no substantive ground to stand on.

What it means in practice is that delegate discretion is bounded by the Atlas rather than plenary: a delegate is a steward exercising judgment on open questions, not a veto-holder over closed ones. Combined with the estoppel rule at A.1.6.6.2, the framework treats a vote as a **representation about the proposal's content** rather than an unconstrained expression of preference.
description: A.1.6.6.1.2 lists it alongside dishonesty and collusion: where a Spell carries nothing new and passes validation, a delegate has no sanctioned discretion to oppose execution.
